key_finding: LATTICE, an LLM-guided hierarchical search index with no embedding model at search time, matches the best fine-tuned ensemble baseline (46.7 nDCG@10) on the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, and a lightweight ensemble reaches 49.1.
methodology: Proposes top-down LLM-guided index construction over multi-level document summaries plus calibrated path-aggregated traversal; evaluated on BRIGHT, NQ, SciFact, SciDocs against embedding+rerank baselines.
why_it_matters: Shows embedding-based top-k retrieval genuinely caps recall on reasoning-intensive queries and that removing the embedder in favor of direct LLM-guided traversal recovers it, directly bearing on what retrieval/reranking substrate an agentic literature-search system should use.
limitations: evaluated on general reasoning-intensive IR benchmarks (BRIGHT) rather than agentic scientific-literature-search benchmarks specifically
sliding-window reranking beats it at low token budgets, so the advantage is budget-dependent
relevance_reason: Directly informs C3 (retrieval/reranking method underlying literature-search agents) and the recall-ceiling question by quantifying where embedding retrieval fails.

key_finding: A bounded pipeline (single seed query, 1.5-hop citation expansion, entailment-based pruning, recency-aware random-walk ranking) outperforms open-ended deep-research agents on proprietary models by up to 3x recall@50 at roughly a third of the cost on LitSearch and a 500K-paper arXiv corpus.
methodology: Structural, inspectable alternative to open-ended agentic search loops; evaluated on LitSearch plus one further benchmark over a fixed arXiv corpus, compared against proprietary deep-research agents.
why_it_matters: Directly answers what agentic move carries the gain (citation-graph traversal + pruning, not open-ended iteration) and challenges the premise that more elaborate agentic loops necessarily beat simpler bounded designs, at lower cost.
limitations: single corpus/domain (arXiv) and two benchmarks
comparison against 'deep research agents' as a class may not cover every agentic design variant
relevance_reason: A bounded citation-graph-traversal design beating full deep-research agents is exactly the kind of evidence the brief asks the scan to hunt for on premise question 2 and 4.

key_finding: PaSa-7B surpasses the best Google-based baseline by 37.78% in recall@20 and 39.90% in recall@50 on RealScholarQuery, and beats PaSa-GPT-4o by 30.36% in recall and 4.25% in precision.
methodology: RL-trained autonomous paper-search agent that invokes search tools, reads papers, and selects references; trained on synthetic AutoScholarQuery (35k queries) and evaluated on newly built RealScholarQuery.
why_it_matters: Establishes the single-query database (Google/Google Scholar) recall ceiling explicitly and quantifies the gap an agentic crawl-and-select design closes, anchoring question 1 and 2 with real numbers.
limitations: trained on synthetic queries sourced from top-tier AI conference papers, so generalization to other scientific fields is untested
gain is reported for the system as a whole rather than cleanly isolating which agentic move (crawling vs. reference selection) drives it
relevance_reason: A landmark system paper directly measuring the baseline-vs-agent recall gap the brief's first two questions are built around, with detailed benchmark construction.

key_finding: WisPaper achieves 22.26% recall on TaxoBench versus 20.92% for an O3 baseline, with its validation module (WisModel) reaching 93.70% validation accuracy against retrieval hallucinations.
methodology: End-to-end agent system combining keyword retrieval with an agentic Deep Search validation module, a library organization module, and a recommendation feed; evaluated on TaxoBench.
why_it_matters: The reported gain over baseline is small (about 1.3 recall points), which is useful counter-evidence to the premise that agentic systems reliably deliver large gains over single-query search.
limitations: TaxoBench construction is not described in the abstract
improvement margin over baseline is modest and could be within noise
relevance_reason: Reports a small agentic-vs-baseline recall gap on a named benchmark, relevant to both the baseline-ceiling and gain-magnitude questions.

key_finding: Across eight expert-designed literature-review projects in physics/astro/cosmology, overlap between human- and AI-selected references was under 6%, and 64% of mid-2025 AI-generated real-paper citations had at least one incorrect metadata field.
methodology: Controlled human-AI comparison study across eight research projects, comparing expert literature selections against ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT Deep Research, and Gemini outputs, with a follow-up single-project test of a 2026 model.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that current agentic literature-search systems reliably match expert search, quantifying both a low overlap ceiling and a high metadata-error rate that any reported 'gain' claim must be checked against.
limitations: applied domain (astrophysics/cosmology) rather than a CS benchmark of agent design itself
small sample (eight projects, one project for the 2026-model follow-up)
relevance_reason: The clearest evidence in the shortlist that agentic literature-search gains do not yet hold up against expert human search, which is exactly what question 4 asks the scan to find.

key_finding: Across six agents on BrowseComp-Plus (validated on BrowseComp), answer accuracy correlates with cumulative retrieval recall, not with number of searches or context consumed, and the best-performing agents issue far fewer redundant queries.
methodology: Trajectory-level diagnosis using human-annotated document-level relevance judgments, decomposing failures into retrieval gaps versus evidence-utilization gaps, with retrieval model and harness held fixed across six agents.
why_it_matters: Directly targets question 2 and 4: it shows that more search effort and more reformulation do not reliably translate into gains, redirecting what should be measured (cumulative recall, stopping criteria) rather than search volume.
limitations: scoped to two closely related benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus/BrowseComp)
retrieval model held fixed, so findings may not generalize across retrieval backends
relevance_reason: Directly diagnoses which agentic moves (reformulation, crawling volume) do and do not carry measured gains, with explicit benchmark methodology — central to questions 2 and 4.

key_finding: ReBOL, which uses LLM query reformulations to seed a Bayesian-optimization posterior over relevance and iteratively acquires document batches for scoring, achieves 46.5% vs 35.0% recall@100 against the best LLM reranker on Robust04.
methodology: Multimodal Bayesian optimization over document relevance initialized by LLM query reformulation, evaluated on five BEIR datasets with two LLMs (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-5.2) against LLM-reranker baselines.
why_it_matters: A concrete retrieval/reranking mechanism that could underlie the retrieval stage of an agentic literature-search system, showing recall gains beyond standard top-k LLM reranking at comparable latency.
limitations: evaluated on general BEIR IR datasets, not a literature-search-agent benchmark or scientific corpus specifically
gain attributed jointly to reformulation and BO modeling rather than isolated to one mechanism
relevance_reason: A retrieval/reranking method that combines query reformulation with iterative relevance modeling, bearing on C3, though tested outside the literature-search setting so capped at 2.

key_finding: In a pre-registered two-arm contrast at 50/500/5000 pages, stripping followable cross-references roughly doubles search cost per grounded fact and leaves some facts unreachable to task-derived search phrasings, while the linked corpus keeps grounded coverage at ceiling with a flat cost curve across two orders of magnitude.
methodology: Pre-registered controlled study on a synthetic wiki-style MCP corpus, comparing an agent's performance with real hyperlinks versus meaning-preserving prose rewrites, over 99 episodes with a Claude agent, recomputed offline from committed run data.
why_it_matters: Quantifies the specific mechanism (link/graph traversal versus search alone) that citation-graph traversal is meant to replicate in literature-search agents, showing cost separation grows with corpus scale — a transferable finding about when graph traversal beats pure search.
limitations: synthetic organizational wiki corpus, not a scholarly citation graph or literature-search benchmark
unusual outlet (Open MIND) and citation count inconsistent with a 2026 preprint, warranting caution about provenance
relevance_reason: Tests the core mechanism behind citation-graph traversal — whether followable links beat search alone — with a controlled, scale-varying design, an explicit method transfer to C2's graph-traversal question even though the corpus is not scholarly.

key_finding: A taxonomy of Deep Research agent architectures (static vs. dynamic workflows, single- vs. multi-agent) with a critical evaluation of current benchmarks identifying restricted external-knowledge access, sequential-execution inefficiencies, and metric-objective misalignment.
methodology: Systematic examination and roadmap paper reviewing information-acquisition strategies, tool-use frameworks (code execution, multimodal input, MCP), and existing benchmarks; abstract-only for methodological detail.
why_it_matters: Its critique of benchmark-metric misalignment directly bears on question 3 — how evaluation sets are built and what their numbers can and cannot support — and should reshape how this scan reads any single benchmark's headline number.
limitations: narrative/taxonomic review rather than new empirical evidence
abstract does not give quantitative findings to weigh against specific systems
relevance_reason: Synthesizes the field's own benchmark critique, which the brief explicitly wants surfaced (question 3), and provides the taxonomy needed to compare agentic designs on like terms.

key_finding: Proposes a four-stage deep-research pipeline (planning, question developing, web exploration, report generation) and summarizes optimization techniques and benchmarks used to evaluate autonomous research agents.
methodology: Systematic survey of the deep-research agent literature organized around the four-stage pipeline; abstract-only for methodological detail.
why_it_matters: Gives a shared vocabulary and stage decomposition (planning vs. exploration vs. synthesis) useful for locating where a reformulation or crawling gain actually occurs, informing question 2's attribution problem.
limitations: narrative survey, no new empirical comparison
overlaps substantially with other deep-research surveys in the shortlist, limiting incremental value
relevance_reason: A second, differently structured survey of the same design space, useful as a synthesis anchor and cross-check on the first survey's taxonomy.

key_finding: PaperQA2 matches or exceeds subject-matter-expert performance on literature retrieval, summarization, and contradiction-detection tasks, writing summaries rated more accurate than existing Wikipedia articles, and identifies 2.34 ± 1.99 contradictions per paper with 70% expert-validated.
methodology: Rigorous human-AI comparison methodology on real-world literature tasks, introducing the LitQA2 hard benchmark used to guide PaperQA2's design; humans given unrestricted internet, search tools, and time.
why_it_matters: This is the strongest existing claim that an agentic system beats expert human search — exactly the premise question 1/2 hinge on — so it sets the bar any replication-failure evidence (like d02cb2e0fab4) must be reconciled against.
limitations: comparison is against human experts rather than against a single-query database baseline directly
biology-heavy contradiction-detection task; generalization across scientific fields not established in the abstract
relevance_reason: A landmark result claiming superhuman literature synthesis with a purpose-built benchmark (LitQA2) — central to testing whether the brief's premise (real agentic gains) actually holds.

key_finding: On Mind2Web 2's 130 long-horizon, citation-backed web-research tasks judged by a tree-structured Agent-as-a-Judge framework, the best system (OpenAI Deep Research) reaches only 50-70% of human performance despite spending half the time.
methodology: New benchmark of 130 realistic long-horizon web-browsing/synthesis tasks built with over 1000 hours of human labor, evaluated via task-specific judge agents assessing correctness and source attribution, across ten frontier systems and humans.
why_it_matters: A rigorous example of benchmark construction (task design, rubric-based judging) directly relevant to question 3, and its 50-70%-of-human ceiling is a concrete instance of reported agentic gains not fully holding up.
limitations: tasks are general web-research/browsing rather than scientific-literature search specifically
Agent-as-a-Judge introduces its own evaluation reliability questions not addressed in the abstract
relevance_reason: Demonstrates careful benchmark construction methodology and a concrete gap between agentic performance and human ceiling, relevant to C4 and C5 even though the task domain is general web search rather than scholarly literature.

key_finding: DynaKRAG, a learned state-conditioned policy coordinating iterative retrieval, query reformulation, and sufficiency checking, ranks first in EM/F1 across nine dataset-backbone pairs on HotpotQA, 2Wiki, and MuSiQue, with 10.1-34.3% token efficiency gains.
methodology: Unified evidence-action RL-style framework with a validity layer, continuation gate, and advantage scorer, evaluated with Qwen2.5-7B, GPT-4o-mini, and Llama-3.1-8B on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Directly models the iterative-retrieval/reformulation/sufficiency-checking loop that agentic literature-search systems also perform, offering a learned coordination policy that could transfer to how such systems decide when to stop crawling.
limitations: evaluated on multi-hop QA benchmarks (HotpotQA, 2Wiki, MuSiQue), not scientific literature search
gains reported relative to matched baselines rather than against a single-query database ceiling
relevance_reason: A method for coordinating exactly the mechanisms (reformulation, iterative retrieval, sufficiency checking) named in C2, but demonstrated outside the literature-search setting, so capped at 2.

key_finding: ReasonIR-8B achieves state-of-the-art 29.9 nDCG@10 (36.9 with reranker) on BRIGHT and improves RAG performance on MMLU (+6.4%) and GPQA (+22.6%) over closed-book baselines.
methodology: Synthetic data generation pipeline pairing documents with challenging reasoning queries and hard negatives; trains an 8B retriever evaluated on BRIGHT and downstream RAG tasks.
why_it_matters: Shows the underlying dense-retriever training technique that agentic literature-search systems would plug in for their retrieval layer, and that query rewriting/test-time compute further boosts recall — bears on which retrieval/reranking method underlies an agent.
limitations: Evaluated on general reasoning-intensive retrieval (BRIGHT, MMLU, GPQA), not a scientific-literature-search agent setting
abstract gives no comparison to single-query database search baseline recall specifically
relevance_reason: State-of-the-art retriever training method relevant to the retrieval/reranking layer underneath agentic literature-search systems (C3), though tested outside the literature-search domain.

key_finding: A three-agent (query/retrieval/learning) hybrid BM25+FAISS system achieves 8.5% higher precision, 7.3% higher recall, and ~210ms lower latency than PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
methodology: FastAPI-based multi-agent architecture with hybrid sparse+dense retrieval and Sentence-Transformers for semantic matching; evaluated against PaperQA and Semantic Scholar.
why_it_matters: A direct, on-domain data point on whether an agentic (query-expansion + retrieval + personalization) design actually beats existing scientific-search baselines, with concrete precision/recall/latency deltas anchoring Q1/Q2.
limitations: No named venue and only 1 citation, so claims are unreplicated
gains attributed to the system as a whole rather than isolated to a specific agentic move
abstract gives no benchmark construction detail
relevance_reason: Directly in scope: a multi-agent scientific-literature-search system reporting quantitative gains over named literature-search baselines (PaperQA, Semantic Scholar).

key_finding: Separating residual-query reformulation (from retrieved evidence) from graph propagation exceeds the strongest baseline by up to 5.59 Recall@5 and 4.50 F1 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA, HotpotQA, and MuSiQue.
methodology: Graph retrieval method that normalizes and combines original-question and residual (evidence-derived) retrieval signals, propagated across entity-sharing propositions; evaluated on three multi-hop QA benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Cleanly isolates the gain from a specific agentic move — evidence-guided query reformulation combined with graph traversal — with a quantified delta, exactly the kind of mechanism attribution Q2 asks for, even though the setting is multi-hop QA rather than paper search.
limitations: Evaluated on general multi-hop QA over Wikipedia, not a scientific-literature corpus or citation graph
no comparison to single-query database search recall ceiling
relevance_reason: Directly attributes a quantified gain to a specific mechanism (evidence-guided reformulation + graph propagation), the exact kind of decomposition Q2 needs, in a closely related graph-retrieval setting.

key_finding: State-of-the-art embedding retriever SFR-Embedding-Mistral scores 59.0 nDCG@10 on MTEB but only 18.3 on BRIGHT's reasoning-intensive queries; explicit query reasoning recovers up to 12.2 points.
methodology: New 1,384-query benchmark spanning economics, psychology, math, and coding, curated from naturally occurring human queries; evaluates existing retrievers and reasoning-augmented variants.
why_it_matters: Establishes that single-query embedding search collapses on reasoning-heavy queries — the baseline-ceiling evidence Q1 needs — and shows the benchmark-construction choices that determine what any later 'agentic' gain is measured against.
limitations: Domains are economics/psychology/math/coding, not curated scientific-literature search
not itself an agentic-system evaluation
relevance_reason: The reference benchmark and baseline-collapse result (59.0→18.3 nDCG) that later reasoning-retrieval and agentic work is measured against; foundational for the recall-ceiling question.

key_finding: Across Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and a custom harness, grep-based retrieval generally outperforms vector retrieval on a 116-question LongMemEval sample, with overall scores driven more by harness/tool-calling style than by retrieval sophistication.
methodology: Two empirical experiments comparing grep vs. dense vector retrieval inside multiple agent harnesses, including a distractor-injection experiment measuring robustness to irrelevant context; abstract-only for exact numbers.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the premise that more sophisticated (vector/embedding) retrieval reliably beats a plain baseline inside an agent loop — the harness and tool-calling paradigm can dominate the retrieval-method choice, exactly the kind of non-replication Q4 asks the scan to surface.
limitations: Setting is conversational-memory agent search (LongMemEval), not scientific-literature retrieval
small 116-question sample
no scientific-corpus or citation-graph component
relevance_reason: A rare finding that a simple baseline (grep) beats the fancier retrieval method inside real agent harnesses — directly relevant to whether agentic sophistication actually carries the reported gains.

key_finding: State-of-the-art LLMs answer only 0.40 accuracy on FRAMES with no retrieval, rising to 0.66 (>50% relative improvement) with a multi-step retrieval pipeline.
methodology: New multi-domain, multi-hop RAG benchmark (FRAMES) unifying factuality, retrieval, and reasoning evaluation; baseline vs. multi-step-retrieval comparison.
why_it_matters: Gives a clean no-retrieval-vs-multi-step-retrieval baseline delta and a worked example of benchmark construction unifying factuality/retrieval/reasoning axes — a useful template for what ceiling number an agentic literature-search system needs to beat.
limitations: General knowledge multi-hop QA, not a scientific-literature-search benchmark
the 'multi-step retrieval pipeline' gain is not decomposed into specific agentic moves
relevance_reason: Reports a clear baseline-vs-iterative-retrieval accuracy gap (0.40→0.66) and details benchmark-construction methodology, both directly useful to Q1/Q3 even though the domain is general RAG rather than literature search.

key_finding: Agents-K1's pipeline converts 2.46 million scientific papers into agent-native knowledge graphs (releasing a 1M-paper subset, Scholar-KG) and reports superior performance on scientific information extraction, KG construction, and multi-hop scientific reasoning.
methodology: Multimodal document parser plus a 4B GRPO-trained extraction model feeding a 'graphanything' CLI agent interface unifying web search, multimodal graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal; abstract-only for quantitative comparisons.
why_it_matters: A concrete, on-domain instantiation of exactly the system design the brief is scanning for — search plus citation-graph traversal over a large scientific corpus — and its released Scholar-KG resource would change what corpus/benchmark a project builds its own agent against.
limitations: Abstract gives no numeric comparison against single-query search or an ablation isolating the traversal component's contribution
'superior performance' claims are unquantified in the abstract
relevance_reason: Directly on-domain: an agent architecture unifying web search, graph retrieval, and cross-document traversal purpose-built for scientific literature, matching the brief's core system-design question.

key_finding: Relocating BrowseComp-Plus's evidence into a 553M-document corpus built without reference to the benchmark drops the strongest agent's evidence recall from 84.3% to 21.4% (answer accuracy falls only 5 points) while search calls rise 63%.
methodology: A dataset-agnostic 'projection' pipeline that decomposes each question into atomic reasoning hops and re-grounds them in an independently built corpus (ClimbMix), retaining only hops verified by automatic checks, an independent agent, and human review; applied to 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions yielding 57 fully grounded questions.
why_it_matters: A direct demonstration that a benchmark's own corpus-construction choices (evidence and distractors selected per query) inflate reported agentic-search performance — exactly the Q4 failure mode the scan is asked to find, and a transferable method for stress-testing any literature-search benchmark's construction.
limitations: BrowseComp-Plus is a general web-browsing/QA benchmark, not a scientific-literature-search benchmark
only 57 of 830 questions survive the strict projection, a large sample-size loss
relevance_reason: Shows a reported agentic-search benchmark result collapsing once corpus construction is decontaminated — a template and cautionary case for the benchmark-construction and gain-replication questions.

key_finding: PaperPilot-9B raises Hit@5 from 58.0 to 77.0, MRR from 47.5 to 59.4, and nDCG@10 from 26.8 to 32.5 over a base toolset agent, while cutting workflow execution errors from 9.5% to 0%, by framing literature search as an executable, user-refinable DAG of operators (keyword search, citation expansion, filtering, reranking, evidence extraction).
methodology: Supervised workflow imitation plus preference optimization over controlled workflow corruptions, trained on Qwen3.5-9B; evaluated in multi-turn interaction against a base toolset agent.
why_it_matters: A directly on-domain system with a clean baseline-to-agentic-workflow delta (Hit@5 +19, MRR +11.9, nDCG@10 +5.7) that decomposes the workflow into named operators including citation expansion — giving Q2 a concrete, attributable mechanism rather than an undifferentiated system-level gain.
limitations: Abstract does not report how the evaluation queries/relevance labels were constructed
gains are for one base model family (Qwen3.5-9B) and may not generalize to other backbones
relevance_reason: A scientific-literature-search agent with an explicit, editable workflow (including citation expansion) and concrete quantitative gains over a baseline toolset agent — squarely the system design and mechanism-attribution the brief is built around.

key_finding: Search-time contamination — deep research agents retrieving benchmark metadata, question context, or ground-truth answers during live web search — inflates measured performance by up to 4% across six public benchmarks.
methodology: Defines three contamination severities (metadata leakage, question-context leakage, explicit-answer leakage) and develops detection algorithms applied to modern deep research agents on six public benchmarks; abstract-only for per-benchmark breakdowns.
why_it_matters: A direct mechanism by which reported agentic-search gains are artefacts of evaluation leakage rather than genuine capability — exactly the kind of inflated-benchmark finding Q4 asks the scan to surface, and argues for contamination-aware practices any literature-search benchmark should adopt.
limitations: Concerns general deep-research-agent benchmarks rather than scientific-literature-search benchmarks specifically
abstract does not specify which of the six benchmarks are literature-related
relevance_reason: Shows reported deep-research-agent performance is partly inflated by search-time leakage, a direct contradiction of the premise that measured agentic gains are real, and a concrete contamination-control practice for benchmark construction.

key_finding: OpenScholar-8B outperforms GPT-4o by 5% and PaperQA2 by 7% in correctness on ScholarQABench (2,967 expert queries, 208 long-form answers across 4 domains), while GPT-4o hallucinates citations 78–90% of the time versus OpenScholar's expert-level citation accuracy.
methodology: Retrieval-augmented LM over a 45M-paper open-access datastore with a self-feedback inference loop; evaluated on the newly introduced ScholarQABench and by human preference judgments against expert-written answers.
why_it_matters: The reference system and benchmark for scientific-literature synthesis: its expert-query benchmark construction (2,967 queries, multi-domain, human-preference evaluation) sets the standard other agentic literature-search systems are measured against, and its closed-book vs. retrieval-augmented comparison anchors the baseline-ceiling question.
limitations: Correctness/citation-accuracy gains are relative to GPT-4o and PaperQA2 rather than a plain single-query search baseline
human preference evaluation (51–70% preferred) is comparative and may not generalize across all four covered domains
relevance_reason: A landmark, directly on-domain retrieval-augmented scientific-literature system with its own purpose-built expert benchmark (ScholarQABench) — foundational reference point for the whole scan.

key_finding: Existing agentic-search benchmarks rely on static, limited corpora and pre-defined gold document sets that fail to elicit or evaluate agentic behavior in dynamic web environments; InfoDeepSeek proposes a query-construction methodology (determinacy, difficulty, diversity) and fine-grained accuracy/utility/compactness metrics instead.
methodology: New benchmark for agentic information seeking over dynamic web environments, with a systematic query-construction protocol and an evaluation framework distinct from static gold-document scoring; tested across multiple LLMs, search engines, and question types.
why_it_matters: A worked critique of exactly the benchmark-construction failure mode Q3/Q4 care about — fixed corpora and gold sets that don't match how agentic systems actually search — offering a construction methodology any literature-search benchmark could adapt.
limitations: Targets general web information-seeking agents, not scientific-literature search specifically
abstract does not report concrete accuracy numbers for individual systems
relevance_reason: Directly addresses how static, gold-set benchmarks misjudge dynamic agentic search, relevant to Q3's benchmark-construction question even though the domain is general web search.

key_finding: GraphRAG frequently underperforms vanilla RAG on many real-world tasks; GraphRAG-Bench systematically maps the conditions (fact retrieval, complex reasoning, summarization, creative generation) under which graph structure does or does not help.
methodology: New benchmark with difficulty-graded tasks and full-pipeline evaluation (graph construction, retrieval, generation) comparing GraphRAG variants against vanilla RAG.
why_it_matters: Directly tests whether the graph-traversal mechanism the brief is watching for actually carries a gain over plain retrieval, and finds it often does not — a concrete instance of Q2/Q4's 'which move carries the gain, and where does it fail to hold' question, even though the graphs here are general knowledge graphs rather than citation graphs.
limitations: Evaluates general knowledge-graph RAG rather than citation-graph traversal over scientific literature
abstract does not give the specific magnitude of GraphRAG's underperformance
relevance_reason: Shows the graph-traversal agentic move — one of the three system-design moves named in the brief — often fails to beat vanilla retrieval, a direct instance of the gain-replication-failure question the scan was asked to reach for.

key_finding: Sparse (keyword-based) retrieval achieves results close to state-of-the-art dense retrieval for biology literature QA, without the infrastructure overhead of dense retrieval.
methodology: LLM-based literature search-and-distillation system evaluated against biology-related questions from existing literature benchmarks, comparing sparse vs dense retrieval and methods to increase document coverage.
why_it_matters: Suggests the recall ceiling of single-query sparse search may already approach that of dense retrieval, undercutting the assumption that agentic/dense pipelines are required to close the gap the brief asks about.
limitations: Evaluated only on biology-domain benchmarks
No explicit numeric recall figures given for the sparse vs dense gap
relevance_reason: Directly tests the baseline recall-ceiling question (C1) and shows sparse search competitive with dense, bearing on the premise the scan must interrogate.

key_finding: NIS-Agent, which applies context isolation to counter a newly identified 'inertia bias' in self-judging agents, matches baseline performance while cutting token cost by 33% across GAIA, WebWalkerQA, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-zh.
methodology: Introduces the IBIS benchmark controlling search observations to isolate inertia bias; evaluates NIS-Agent and a fine-tuned 8B model across four deep-research benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Identifies a specific architectural failure mode (self-authored action history biasing later judgment) that helps explain why agentic gains vary across systems and designs, relevant to isolating which agentic moves actually help versus hurt.
limitations: Benchmarks are general web/QA tasks (GAIA, BrowseComp) rather than scientific literature search specifically
No explicit single-query baseline recall comparison given
relevance_reason: Relevant to C2 by isolating a specific mechanism (context isolation) and its measured effect in agentic search systems, though its setting is general web research rather than scientific literature.

key_finding: Deep Research Bench's frozen 'RetroSearch' corpus of 89 human-verified multi-step web research tasks lets offline agents be evaluated comparably to live-web agents, enabling reliable tracking of hallucination, tool use, and forgetting over time.
methodology: 89 task instances across 8 categories with human-derived answers, a frozen scraped-web corpus, and automated trace evaluation; benchmarks major LLMs and branded 'Deep Research' products.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a reproducible way to construct research-agent benchmarks that control for the ever-changing web, directly informing how literature-search benchmarks should be built to avoid drift and enable fair comparison.
limitations: Tasks are general web research, not scientific literature database retrieval specifically
Corpus freezing may not transfer cleanly to scholarly database search behavior
relevance_reason: A strong exemplar of rigorous benchmark construction (C4) for research agents, closely analogous to literature-search benchmark design.

key_finding: LitSearch finds a 24.8-point absolute recall@5 gap between BM25 and state-of-the-art dense retrievers, LLM-based reranking adds a further 4.4% over the best dense retriever, and commercial search engines lag the best dense retriever by 32 points.
methodology: 597 realistic literature-search queries built from GPT-4-generated questions on inline-citation paragraphs plus author-written queries about their own recent papers, expert-reviewed; benchmarks retrieval and reranking models.
why_it_matters: Directly establishes the baseline recall ceiling (BM25 vs dense) the scan needs to anchor any reported agentic improvement against, and its construction methodology is a template for benchmark quality (C4).
limitations: Restricted to ML/NLP literature
Queries are partly LLM-generated, which may not fully capture real researcher intents
relevance_reason: Answers decision 1 (recall ceiling) and decision 3 (benchmark construction) directly with numbers, making it foundational to the scan's core questions.

key_finding: Across 35 included AI-scientist systems, only 38% release novelty-verification methods and none of nine closed-loop (L4) systems demonstrates an externally validated in-loop oracle.
methodology: Survey screening 125 candidate works with full-text coding of 26 systems across seven audit dimensions (autonomy, evaluation, artifacts, human-in-loop, novelty verification).
why_it_matters: Warns that claims from autonomous research/literature-search agents are largely unverified externally, a reason to treat reported agentic gains skeptically until independently checked, directly bearing on decision 4.
limitations: Covers the full AI-scientist lifecycle, not literature search specifically
Abstract gives no numeric detail on literature-search subsystem performance
relevance_reason: As a review, it flags a systemic verification gap bearing on whether reported gains hold up, though its scope extends beyond literature search alone.

key_finding: HySemRAG's structured field extraction achieves 35.1% higher semantic similarity than PDF chunking (0.655 vs 0.485, p<0.000001), and its agentic self-correction mechanism achieves 68.3% single-pass success with 99.0% citation accuracy.
methodology: Eight-stage pipeline combining hybrid retrieval (semantic search, keyword filtering, KG traversal), agentic self-correction, and citation verification; evaluated across 643 observations from 60 testing sessions, applied to geospatial epidemiology literature.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates a concrete hybrid-retrieval-plus-agentic-self-correction design with measured gains, providing evidence on which specific components drive quality in literature-synthesis systems.
limitations: Applied domain example (ozone/cardiovascular epidemiology) rather than a general literature-search benchmark
No comparison to single-query baseline search recall
relevance_reason: Directly relevant to C2 and C3 — hybrid retrieval and agentic self-correction with measured performance deltas in a literature-synthesis system.

key_finding: PaSaMaster achieves a 16.5x higher F1-score than Google Scholar and a 37.8% higher F1-score than GPT-5.2 at about 1% of the cost, reducing source hallucination from 32.66% to zero, across 38 disciplines in PaSaMaster-Bench.
methodology: Recursive self-evolving agentic retrieval system with self-evolving intent refinement, hallucination-free ranking over verified papers, and planning/retrieval separation between frontier and lightweight LLMs; evaluated on PaSaMaster-Bench.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the agentic gain over baseline single-query search (Google Scholar) attributable to specific mechanisms (self-evolving retrieval, verified-paper ranking), exactly the comparison decisions 1 and 2 need.
limitations: Preprint with 0 citations; gains not yet independently verified
Benchmark (PaSaMaster-Bench) construction details not given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Provides the sharpest example of an agentic literature-retrieval system quantifying gain over baseline database search and attributing it to specific mechanisms.

key_finding: On BrowseComp-Plus's fixed, human-verified corpus, Search-R1 with BM25 achieves only 3.86% accuracy versus GPT-5's 55.9%, rising to 70.1% when GPT-5 is paired with a Qwen3-Embedding retriever using fewer search calls.
methodology: Benchmark derived from BrowseComp using a fixed curated corpus with human-verified supporting documents and mined hard negatives, enabling controlled disentanglement of retriever vs. reasoning-model contributions.
why_it_matters: Gives a controlled, corpus-fixed measurement of the accuracy/recall ceiling of a plain retriever (BM25) versus stronger retrievers and reasoning models — exactly the anchor decision 1 needs — and shows how uncontrolled live-web benchmarks can misattribute gains.
limitations: Domain is general web deep-research (BrowseComp-derived), not scientific literature databases specifically
Corpus curation choices could still bias which documents count as 'hard negatives'
relevance_reason: Central to C1, C3, and C4: quantifies the baseline BM25 ceiling, evaluates retrieval methods, and demonstrates rigorous, contamination-resistant benchmark construction.

key_finding: Search-based agents directly find ground-truth-labeled evaluation data on HuggingFace for roughly 3% of questions on HLE, SimpleQA, and GPQA, and accuracy on that contaminated subset drops about 15% once HuggingFace is blocked.
methodology: Analysis of search-based agent logs on three capability benchmarks identifying leaked evaluation-dataset sources during retrieval, with an ablation blocking HuggingFace access.
why_it_matters: Shows that part of a search agent's apparent capability gain is an artifact of retrieval surfacing the answer key itself, directly undermining trust in reported agentic gains unless benchmark construction controls for this — exactly decision 4's concern.
limitations: Benchmarks studied (HLE, SimpleQA, GPQA) are general capability tests, not scientific-literature-search benchmarks specifically
Contamination measured only via HuggingFace hosting, likely an undercount of the true issue
relevance_reason: The clearest demonstration in the shortlist of a reported search-agent gain partly evaporating once a contamination source is controlled for, directly answering decision 4.

key_finding: CG-RAG's Lexical-Semantic Graph Retrieval (LeSeGR), integrating sparse and dense signals within citation graphs, significantly outperforms RAG methods paired with state-of-the-art retrievers on research question-answering benchmarks.
methodology: Contextual graph representation of citation graphs combined with hybrid lexical-semantic graph retrieval and graph-aware generation, evaluated across multiple research-QA benchmarks and domains.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the citation-graph-traversal mechanism named in decision 2, showing hybrid graph+lexical+semantic retrieval as the specific move that improves over plain RAG retrieval.
limitations: Abstract does not report the size of the gain over a single-query baseline
Benchmark domains and construction not detailed in the abstract
relevance_reason: Matches decision 2 and C3 precisely: citation-graph traversal combined with hybrid sparse/dense retrieval, exactly the mechanism the brief asks about.

key_finding: OpenNovelty, deployed on 500+ ICLR 2026 submissions, uses a four-phase retrieval-and-comparison pipeline to produce evidence-grounded novelty reports, preliminarily surfacing closely related prior work authors may have missed.
methodology: Agentic pipeline: query extraction, semantic-search retrieval of prior work, taxonomy construction, and full-text contribution comparison; abstract-only, no quantitative retrieval evaluation given.
why_it_matters: Illustrates a downstream application of literature-retrieval agents (peer-review novelty checking) rather than literature-search evaluation itself, of marginal direct use for the scan's core recall/benchmark/mechanism questions.
limitations: Focused on novelty assessment for peer review, not literature-search benchmarking
No recall/precision numbers or benchmark comparison reported
relevance_reason: Uses agentic literature retrieval as a component but targets a different task (novelty assessment), offering only tangential evidence on the brief's core questions.

key_finding: ReMindRAG's LLM-guided graph traversal with memory-replay, storing traversal experience in KG edge embeddings, outperforms existing KG-RAG baselines in a train-free manner across benchmark datasets.
methodology: Node exploration/exploitation plus memory-replay traversal over knowledge-graph edge embeddings, compared against existing KG-RAG baselines and LLM backbones; abstract-only for quantitative detail.
why_it_matters: Offers a graph-traversal retrieval technique (memory-based, cost-efficient) structurally similar to the citation-graph traversal mechanisms literature-search agents use, though demonstrated on general knowledge graphs rather than citation graphs.
limitations: Evaluated on general knowledge graphs, not citation graphs or scientific literature corpora
No explicit numeric gains reported in the abstract
relevance_reason: A general-purpose graph-traversal RAG technique relevant by analogy to citation-graph traversal, capped for being off the brief's literature-search setting.

key_finding: An agent dynamically choosing between GraphRAG and VectorRAG, tuned via Direct Preference Optimization, gains 0.63 in Context Recall and 0.56 in Context Precision over baseline on synthetic literature-review benchmarks, with additional gains in faithfulness and answer relevance.
methodology: Pipeline ingesting PubMed/arXiv/Google Scholar metadata into a Neo4j citation knowledge graph and a FAISS vector store; a Llama-3.3-70B agent selects GraphRAG vs VectorRAG per query, instruction-tuned via DPO, evaluated with bootstrapped metrics on synthetic query benchmarks.
why_it_matters: Directly attributes measured gains to specific agentic and retrieval choices (dynamic GraphRAG/VectorRAG selection, DPO instruction tuning, hybrid reranking) in a scientific-literature-review system, giving concrete evidence for decision 2 and C3.
limitations: Evaluated on synthetic benchmarks mimicking real queries rather than a human-curated literature-search benchmark
No comparison to a plain single-query baseline recall ceiling
relevance_reason: A close, on-topic system paper combining citation-graph traversal, hybrid retrieval, and agentic query routing with quantified gains, directly informing the brief's system-design and mechanism questions.

key_finding: Introduces DeepResearch Bench, 100 PhD-level research tasks across 22 fields crafted by domain experts, with a reference-based adaptive-criteria scoring method and a separate framework measuring effective citation count and citation accuracy for deep research agents.
methodology: Benchmark construction paper: 100 expert-crafted tasks across 22 domains, plus two evaluation methodologies (report-quality scoring, citation-accuracy assessment) validated for alignment with human judgment. Abstract-only for validation numbers.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete, expert-labeled construction method for literature/research-agent benchmarks and a citation-accuracy metric that could be used to test whether reported agentic gains hold on an independently built set — directly informs how we judge benchmark comparability (decision 3) and gives a metric candidate for probing replication failure (decision 4).
limitations: targets general 'deep research' report generation rather than literature-search retrieval specifically
no baseline single-query recall figures reported
abstract does not give quantitative alignment or gain numbers
relevance_reason: Directly addresses benchmark construction for agentic research/literature agents, including a citation-accuracy evaluation framework relevant to retrieval quality assessment.
